demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again
I remind myself it could have been worse
I dwell on what I have done wrong

Threat.value: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
I feel isolated and set apart from others
The person I have become is unrecognisable to me

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm as a coping strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is the only markedly high-risk/impulsive strategy and is poorly supported by the rest of the selected nodes. The other strategies are comparatively cognitive/obsessional (mental rituals, downward comparison), and the threat/memory/appraisal items do not show the broader dysregulation, dissociation, or severe affective overload that would make this combination clinically cohesive.

issues.item: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
issues.explanation: Pain recall implies the patient was physically injured in the traumatic event. That is hard to reconcile with the trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another' unless she was also injured, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere in the profile. The rest of the memory items emphasize fragmented retrieval and sensory reliving, but not a personally injured trauma narrative.

vignette: Amara, 47, stood on the upper deck of the midtown renovation project when the temporary bracing gave way. She had double-checked the load calculations, but a miscalculation in the live load estimation had been enough. The scaffolding groaned, shifted, and sent a seasoned drywall contractor crashing through the safety net. The sickening thud, the cry, the blood on the concrete-it was all too real. She had caused it. Her own oversight had left a man broken. In the weeks that followed, Amara's life narrowed. The blueprints she once loved became impossible to navigate; her eyes skittered across the drafting table, unable to hold a line. When she tried to deliberately pull the accident from her mind, the memory slipped away like smoke, leaving only a sour metallic taste in her mouth whenever it suddenly returned. She began to hear the groan of bending steel in the quiet of her suburban home. Her conviction that she was fundamentally different from anyone else who might have been there pushed her toward self-blame rumination and silent mental rituals. Because she believed she alone was responsible, she told herself it could have been worse, using downward comparison to ground herself. Yet this negative appraisal did not isolate her from the past; it actively pulled the memory forward, forcing it to the surface whenever she felt disconnected. When the memory returned, carrying its metallic taste and phantom groan, it immediately spiked her threat response. Her body braced for collapse, and the false alarms made ordinary sounds feel like structural failures. This heightened alarm state, in turn, made it nearly impossible to deliberately recall the event, leaving the memory to fracture into sensory flashes. Each time the memory slipped through, it reinforced her conviction that she was unrecognizable and set apart from everyone else. The negative appraisals then looped back to demand more rituals, as she felt compelled to perform mental counting to stave off the panic. But the rituals themselves kept the memory just out of reach, preventing deliberate integration while allowing the taste and sounds to intrude. And when the memory finally broke through fully, it sent her startle reflex into overdrive, proving to her that her threat response was permanently broken. The false alarms forced her into further downward comparisons and mental counting, which only deepened the self-blame. The self-blame confirmed her isolation, and the isolation made the negative appraisals feel like absolute truth. She knew the mental rituals and self-comparisons were futile, yet they only kept the memory fragmented and the threat network humming. Every ritual she performed fed the memory's fragments, and every memory fragment lit up the threat network, which in turn sharpened her negative self-appraisals. Now, four months post-event, Amara sits in her husband's study, the silence of their home pressing against her. She has stopped visiting construction sites, taking sick leave under the guise of exhaustion. The mental rituals have become a prison; she counts the rivets on the ceiling fan to avoid panic, yet the count never satisfies. She knows, with a quiet desperation, that the loop is closing. What finally brought her to seek help was not the startle responses or the taste of copper, but the realization that she was drifting through her own marriage like a ghost, unable to look her husband in the eye without feeling the phantom weight of the scaffold on her shoulders. She is afraid she will never stop bracing for a collapse that already happened, but she is hoping, desperately, to find a way to remember the event without the memory hijacking her life.
